victims.description: Pedigo Products, Inc. is a privately held American manufacturer of stainless steel and chromium medical equipment for the healthcare industry. It disregards its own security, as well as that of its customers and employees, and makes no attempt to negotiate agreements to prevent data leaks. As a result, we provide you with 1.3 TB of sensitive corporate data, such as: carrier account numbers, customer-specific pricing, commission adjustments, customs/MDEL identifiers and customer/employee contact information, customer contracts, price and discount schedules, shipping and routing instructions, employee and customer personal data, FDA quality records (DMR, DHR, DHF, CAPA, complaints, MDR), CAD files and trade secrets, intellectual property and non-disclosure agreements, financial statements, tax returns, payroll records, bank details, and legal documents. Contractual obligations to customers and confidentiality, as well as HIPAA/GDPR/CCPA/PIPEDA regulations, were violated. We urge the authorities to pay attention to these issues. Due to Pedigo's negligence, it will also suffer losses in the form of loss of trade secrets and intellectual property protection, copying by competitors, loss of business with hospitals and dealers, and serious reputational and financial damage.

Valenti Management is known as the Tampa-based Wendy's franchise operator. They are extremely lax when it comes to cybersecurity and are unwilling to cooperate in preventing data leaks, which is why we offer you commercial and confidential documents such as: price lists and discount agreements with key suppliers/distributors; new product/menu launch plans and marketing strategies; franchise and partnership contracts; terms of supplier discounts and promotions; employee personal data (Social Security numbers, wage data, taxes, benefits, medical records); financial statements, tax returns, bank statements, and debt agreements; real estate leases, construction contracts, and area development plans; customer loyalty program and payment card data; supply chain logistics data, inventory, and confidential operational data; litigation, insurance, and internal audit files. As a result, they will lose their reputation with clients and employees and face legal action due to the leak.

A private ophthalmology clinic specializing in various fields. However, it completely fails to ensure the security of itself and its clients and is extremely lax in its recordkeeping. The structure of its confidential records is determined by the categories of protected health information (PHI) it creates and stores. Because Concord Eye Center makes no attempt to regulate security, we provide you with the following information: patient identification and administrative data: this includes names, addresses, dates of birth, social security numbers, and contact information; clinical and medical history: detailed symptom records, ophthalmological and systemic medical history, and family history; diagnostic and lab results; surgical and treatment documentation; billing and financial information: insurance information, claims data, and payment records. Leaking these documents would primarily violate the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) and the HITECH Act, which provide for tiered civil penalties for each category of violation, leading to distrust of their business by customers and partners and its collapse.

Greentech Environmental LLC, a manufacturer of air purification systems using patented ODOGard and ARC technologies, has failed to fully secure and address the breach, and therefore we are publishing their confidential information such as (intellectual property/trade secrets, financial statements, employee data, operational/strategic plans, legal documents, corporate governance documents, and manufacturing drawings) that would violate the Defend Trade Secrets Act (CFAA) and state privacy laws, which would subject us to injunctive relief, treble damages, penalties, mandatory notification, class action lawsuits, loss of patent rights and competitive advantage, and possible business failure.

ECF, Inc., a piping and insulation contractor specializing in the design and construction of terminals for the transshipment of liquid hydrocarbons such as asphalt, crude oil, and renewable fuels, has completely failed to ensure the security of its systems and is unwilling to compromise. Therefore, we are providing you with access to confidential information (proprietary pipeline designs, CAD drawings, customer lists, pricing models, financial data, employee information, and trade secrets), which violates the Complaints and Abuse Act (CFAA) and state civil liability laws and may result in injunctions, damages, fines, mandatory notices, class actions, loss of competitive advantage, and possibly termination of operations.

Nu-Quest Distribution Inc. is a privately held pharmaceutical wholesaler based in Newfoundland and Labrador. The company specializes in the distribution of brand-name and generic medications, as well as medical devices. Its negligent attitude toward security and unwillingness to negotiate led to the leak of confidential documents, including supplier/customer pricing and price lists, drug transaction and compliance records, financial statements, employee personnel files, and legal documents. Due to our disclosure of these details, the company faces regulatory fines, license revocation, lawsuits, and damage to its competition and reputation.

placer.ai Revenue $136.5 Million private US company valued at $1.5 billion that sells foot traffic analytics for physical locations, estimating visits to stores, malls and offices from anonymized data on tens of millions of mobile phones with 92%+ claimed accuracy. It hit $100 million annual recurring revenue in 2024 after growing 80% in a year and serves 4,000+ customers including Sony, Wegmans, BJ's Wholesale, SeaWorld and Bloomberg, which puts Placer data into its Terminal so investors can track company performance before earnings. Money comes from SaaS subscriptions starting around $12,000 a year, API data feeds and add-on datasets, and it has raised $268 million in total funding. Around 630 employees work at Placer.ai after 150 layoffs in January 2025 aimed at reaching profitability, and it owns no factories or stores because its product is pure software and data.

bigid.com Revenue $100 Million BigID is the enterprise data security platform that finds and classifies sensitive data across cloud apps, databases and files, showing where private data lives and who can access it. It now focuses on AI, spotting shadow AI tools and checking what data Copilots and agents reach, and in September 2026 launched AgentIQ letting AI assistants trigger data cleanup and access reviews from Claude, Copilot or ChatGPT. It serves hundreds of enterprise clients like Telenor and Fiserv, one of which deleted 27,000 sensitive records from 2.5 petabytes of storage. Money comes from enterprise subscriptions priced per data source, with $175K as one AWS Marketplace benchmark. Around 600 employees work there after cutting 150 roles in May 2026 to go AI-first. It raised $320M at a $1B+ valuation and owns no factories or stores.

confluent.io Revenue $1.16 Billion Confluent is the enterprise data streaming platform built on Apache Kafka that lets companies process live events like payments, orders and sensor data in real time, and it is now owned by IBM which bought it for about $11 billion in March 2026. It ended 2025 with 6,690 customers including roughly 40% of the Fortune 500 and grew revenue 21% with its cloud segment alone growing 27%. Customers include BMW, L'Oreal, Michelin and Ticketmaster and the platform runs across 60+ cloud regions on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Money comes from cloud usage and software subscriptions, about 96% of revenue, paid for compute and data transfer rather than per-seat fees. Around 3,241 employees worked at Confluent across 27 countries before the IBM deal and it owns no factories or stores because its product is pure software and cloud. Confluent was still unprofitable with a $295 million loss in 2025 though it earned positive operating income excluding stock pay.

moneygram.com Revenue $2.1 Billion MoneyGram global money transfer network moving nearly $200 billion a year through almost 500,000 retail agent locations in 200+ countries and serving 60 million+ active customers, with over 70% of transactions now digital. It earns mainly from transfer fees plus currency exchange spreads, not from owning stores, since almost all locations are partner agents like post offices and grocery chains. In 2025 it cut 449 jobs to speed up digital growth and in 2026 launched its own MGUSD dollar stablecoin and a Visa card that spends digital dollars anywhere Visa works. MoneyGram owns no factories or stores, it is a licensed money transmitter with 75+ regulatory approvals, around 2,000 employees in 36 countries, and was taken private in 2023 for $1.8 billion.

kfc.com Revenue $36.4 Billion KFC runs 34,747 restaurants across 150+ countries and about 99% are franchised, run by local partners, serving roughly 1 billion chickens every year. Its restaurants sold $36.4 billion of food in 2025 with $1.5 billion in operating profit, earned mainly from 4-6% sales royalties paid by franchisees, not from selling chicken. 2025 was a record year with nearly 3,000 new restaurants opened across 105 countries, roughly one new KFC every 3 hours and 10,000 stores added in the last 5 years. KFC owns zero chicken farms or factories and buys from suppliers like Tyson Foods and Pilgrim's Pride with fresh deliveries up to 3 times a week. Around 30,000 corporate employees work for KFC worldwide while over 1 million people work across its franchise restaurants and supply network. A new U.S. KFC does about $1.5 million in average annual sales per restaurant and KFC is the world's #1 chicken chain by locations and sales.

The Health Sciences Centre in Winnipeg, one of the largest medical institutions, was targeted by us that resulted in the largest data breach among healthcare institutions. Our group chose not to completely disrupt the facility’s operations, recognizing the potentially devastating consequences that such an action could have had on patients’ lives and health. Nevertheless, Health Sciences Centre management stated that no sensitive data had been affected, despite having been informed otherwise. The data included, but was not limited to, the following information: Patient medical records: Full name, date of birth, address and phone number Hospital medical record number Diagnoses, medical history, allergies and medications Laboratory results, imaging reports Appointment dates, treatment details and physician information. Employee and healthcare professional information: Names, contact details, dates of birth and employee numbers Employment, payroll and banking information Professional credentials, work schedules and departmental assignments. Financial and insurance information: Billing records and payment histories Insurance or benefits claim information. Confidential hospital documents: Internal emails and staff communications System configurations, network diagrams and security procedures Database backups and exported spreadsheets. We would have very much preferred to avoid making this data breach public, but the management has left us with no other choice.
